acceptedReports.priceScope: Whole-organization cost per match against long-run earnings from the BBBS mentoring trial follow-up; income-only welfare comparison, not a verified marginal gift offer

what: Big Brothers Big Sisters Lone Star matches children facing adversity with screened volunteer mentors who meet them regularly, in community-based, school-based and Amachi (children of incarcerated parents) programs.
It is a Texas agency based in Dallas whose core markets include Greater Houston, where the program has run since the 1950s; it served 5,110 children in 2024.

This in-depth review prices the organization’s whole cost per match against long-run earnings from a tax-record follow-up of Big Brothers Big Sisters’ randomized trial, in which Houston was one of eight sites.
strengths: The 1991–93 randomized trial of about 1,100 youth found behavior improvements while matched; linked tax records show treatment youth were significantly more likely to attend college.
A larger observational comparison of unmatched applicants found earnings about 19% higher at ages 20 to 25, and Arnold Ventures rates community-based mentoring Near Top Tier.
Volunteers provide the mentoring, so cash costs are low: about $2,900 per child served a year today.
reservations: Our working estimate is about $605K per better life; all of it is income, and the randomized trial’s own earnings estimate is imprecise.
The strongest earnings evidence is observational; we treat half of it as causal.
The trial tested community-based matches in 1991–93; today’s mix includes school-based mentoring, which has weaker evidence.

sections.what: Big Brothers Big Sisters Lone Star (EIN 75-0800632) is the Big Brothers Big Sisters agency for much of Texas, including Greater Houston, Dallas–Fort Worth and, from 2026, Austin. Volunteers are screened and matched one-to-one with school-age children and meet regularly for activities, with professional match-support staff. Programs include community-based, school-based and Amachi Texas mentoring for children of incarcerated parents. It served 5,110 children in 2024. A donation supports the whole organization.
sections.monitoring: Big Brothers Big Sisters of America ran a randomized waitlist trial at eight agencies, including Houston, in 1991–93; 1,138 families consented. Bell and Petkova linked 883 participants to tax records (Treasury data) to measure adult outcomes, and a 2025 version adds an observational comparison of Boston applicants. The agency reports children served through GuideStar. We did not find Houston-only counts or cost per match; we have not contacted the organization.
sections.qualitative: Within 18 months, the original trial found lower absenteeism and fewer school suspensions among matched youth. The long-run follow-up finds treatment youth significantly more likely to attend college, with imprecise earnings effects in the RCT itself. Comparing matched with unmatched applicants, it finds about 19% higher earnings at ages 20 to 25, and the Policy Impacts library records an estimated $56,000 lifetime earnings gain and a negative net government cost. Average adult wages in the sample were low ($16,500 for men, $14,000 for women at ages 25 to 30), so a given percentage gain is a modest dollar amount.
sections.cost:
Our central estimate is **$605K per better life**, using ten healthy-year welfare equivalents. It is an income-only comparison: we credit no health gain.

**Cost.** CY2023 expense was $14.8M for 5,110 children served in 2024, about $2,889 per child a year; at 1.5 years per match that is $4,334 per match. The trial agencies spent about $2,778 per active match in 2018 dollars.

**Benefit.** We credit an 8% gross earnings gain on a $20,000 base from age 20 for 25 years, 60% as net welfare: under half the observational 19%, because the RCT’s own earnings estimate is imprecise. We keep 0.5 for causality, 0.6 for transfer to today’s program mix, 0.9 for displacement and 0.8 for Houston residence.

**Range.** At the trial’s cost the estimate is $738K per better life. Treating the 19% observational effect as fully causal gives $131K per better life; a 3% effect gives $1.59M per better life; gains lasting only ten years give $1.23M per better life. If there is no lasting earnings effect, there is no credited benefit.
sections.funding: Big Brothers Big Sisters Lone Star reported CY2023 revenue of $15.9M, almost all contributions, and expenses of $14.8M, up from $13.1M in 2022 and $12.1M in 2021. A match also needs a volunteer, so whether money alone adds matches is unverified.

model.costScope: CY2023 whole-organization expense per child served (2024) × 1.5 years per match.
model.geographicAttribution: Houston-area children; 0.8 of adult earning years in the Houston metro.
model.formula: Price = 10 × cost per match ÷ [0.5 × discounted years(25, from age 20) × ln(1 + 0.6 × 8% × base ÷ base) × causal × transfer × non-displacement × Houston share]. Health = 0.
model.attribution: A gift is credited with the average effect of an added match at whole-organization cost; volunteer supply is a binding constraint not modeled.
model.uncertainty: Dominated by whether the observational earnings effect is causal and how long it lasts, then transfer to school-based matches.
model.nativeOutcomes: College attendance, adult earnings (ages 20–30), incarceration, teen birth from tax and vital records.

incomePathways.rationale: Long-run tax-record follow-up of the 1991-93 eight-site BBBS randomized trial (Houston was a site): college attendance significantly higher; earnings effects imprecise in the RCT, about 19% at ages 20-25 in a larger observational comparison. Credited as an 8% gross gain from age 20 for 25 years, half treated as causal, net of taxes and lost benefits.
